Why Are Maps Useful?

Textbook page 2 • Launch Lab

📖 Easy Explanation

A map can help people find their way without getting lost.

The Launch Lab asks you to compare written directions with a map for getting from the science classroom to the cafeteria.

Where you are→MAP→Where you want to go

👀 Look at the textbook visual

  • The students are working with directions.
  • The activity changes written directions into a map.
⭐ Remember: A map can make a route easier to understand.
Lesson 1 • Maps

Understanding Maps

Textbook page 2

📖 Easy Explanation

People use different maps for different purposes. The textbook gives examples such as road maps, rail maps, and weather maps.

A map is a flat representation of an area of Earth.

Earth / Place→represented on a flat map
⭐ Remember: Different maps can show different information.
Lesson 1 • Maps

Map View

Textbook page 2 • Figure 1

📖 Easy Explanation

A map view is drawn as if you are looking down from above.

The textbook says a map view can also be called a plan view.

MAP VIEW = ABOVE ↓

👀 Look at the textbook visual

  • Look at the floor-plan drawing on the left.
  • It shows the house from above.
⭐ Remember: Map view = plan view = looking down from above.
Lesson 1 • Maps

Profile View

Textbook page 2 • Figure 1

📖 Easy Explanation

A profile view shows an object as though you are looking at it from the side.

PROFILE VIEW = SIDE →

The same house can look very different depending on the view.

👀 Look at the textbook visual

  • Look at the house drawing on the right.
  • You see the front/side shape, not the floor plan.
⭐ Remember: Profile view = looking from the side.

Map Legend

Textbook page 3 • Figure 2

📖 Easy Explanation

Maps use symbols to represent features.

A map legend, or key, lists the symbols used on the map and explains what they mean.

Symbol→Legend / Key→Meaning

👀 Look at the textbook visual

  • Find the legend on the right side of the park map.
  • The textbook example shows that a dashed line represents a trail.
⭐ Remember: Legend = explains the symbols on a map.
Lesson 1 • Maps

What Is a Map Scale?

Textbook pages 3–4

📖 Easy Explanation

A map scale is the relationship between a distance on the map and the actual distance on the ground.

MAP DISTANCE ↔ ACTUAL DISTANCE

Maps are usually smaller than the real places they represent, so scale is needed.

⭐ Remember: Scale compares map distance with real distance.
Lesson 1 • Maps

Three Ways to Show Scale

Textbook page 3 • Figure 3

📖 Easy Explanation

Scale TypeTextbook Example
Written scaleOne centimeter is equal to one kilometer.
Ratio / fraction1 : 100,000
Graphic scaleA scale bar marked in kilometers

👀 Look at the textbook visual

  • The same road map shows three different ways to express scale.
  • The graphic scale is a bar that can be used when measuring distance.
⭐ Remember: Scale can be written, shown as a ratio, or shown as a graphic bar.

Scale Practice

Textbook page 4 • Math Skills

📖 Easy Explanation

The textbook gives this practice scale:

1 cm : 1 km

If two points are 3 cm apart on the map:

3 cm on map→3 × 1 km→3 km actual distance

This uses only the scale given in the textbook practice.

⭐ Remember: Use the map scale to convert map distance to actual distance.

Scale and Models

Textbook page 4 • Figure 4

📖 Easy Explanation

Models can also be built using scaled measurements.

The textbook explains that models have the same relative proportions as the real objects they represent.

Figure 4 shows different scales, including 1:25 and 12:1.

A Grid System for Plotting Locations

Textbook page 5

📖 Easy Explanation

Mapmakers use two sets of imaginary lines around Earth:

Latitude
Longitude

The intersection of a latitude line and a longitude line can pinpoint a location on a map or globe.

Latitude+Longitude→Location

👀 Look at the textbook visual

  • The globe diagrams show two different sets of imaginary lines.
  • Together they form a grid for locating places.
⭐ Remember: Latitude + Longitude = a specific location.
Lesson 1 • Maps

Longitude

Textbook page 5

📖 Easy Explanation

Longitude is the distance in degrees east or west of the prime meridian.

  • The prime meridian is 0° longitude.
  • It passes through Greenwich, England.
  • The 180° meridian is on the other half of the circle.
  • All meridians pass through the North Pole and South Pole.
Longitude → E / W of Prime Meridian

👀 Look at the textbook visual

  • The longitude diagram shows pole-to-pole lines.
  • The prime meridian is marked as the starting line.
⭐ Remember: Longitude = east / west of the Prime Meridian.
Lesson 1 • Maps

Latitude

Textbook page 5

📖 Easy Explanation

Latitude is the distance in degrees north or south of the equator.

  • The equator divides Earth into the northern and southern hemispheres.
  • Lines of latitude are parallel.
  • The equator is the largest circle; the others become smaller closer to the poles.
Latitude → N / S of Equator

👀 Look at the textbook visual

  • The latitude diagram shows circles around Earth.
  • The equator is the center line.
⭐ Remember: Latitude = north / south of the Equator.
Lesson 1 • Maps

Plotting Locations with Degrees

Textbook page 6

📖 Easy Explanation

Latitude and longitude are measured in degrees.

  • North Pole = 90°N
  • South Pole = 90°S
  • Longitude is measured east or west of the prime meridian.
  • 180°E and 180°W are the same longitude.

The textbook says latitude is always stated before longitude.

👀 Look at the textbook visual

  • The MiniLab globe uses a grid to identify city locations.
  • Read latitude first, then longitude.
⭐ Remember: When writing a location: Latitude first → Longitude second.
Lesson 1 • Maps

Degrees, Minutes, and Seconds

Textbook page 6

📖 Easy Explanation

For more accurate locations, each degree can be divided into smaller parts.

1 degree = 60 minutes (′)
1 minute = 60 seconds (″)

The textbook uses degrees, minutes, and seconds to locate places more accurately.

⭐ Remember: Degree → 60 minutes → each minute has 60 seconds.
Lesson 1 • Maps

Time Zones

Textbook page 7 • Figure 6

📖 Easy Explanation

As Earth rotates, the Sun is directly above different locations at different times.

A time zone is an area where people use the same time.

  • The reference point is the prime meridian.
  • Earth is divided into 24 time zones.
  • A width of 15° longitude equals a difference of 1 hour.
  • Time-zone boundaries do not always follow meridians exactly because they can be changed at political boundaries.

👀 Look at the textbook visual

  • The map shows different bands of time around the world.
  • The textbook visual check compares New York City and Los Angeles.
⭐ Remember: 24 time zones • 15° longitude = 1 hour.
Lesson 1 • Maps

International Date Line

Textbook page 7

📖 Easy Explanation

The line of longitude 180° east or west of the prime meridian is called the International Date Line.

Crossing DirectionWhat the textbook says
East → WestIt is the next day in the west.
West → EastIt is the day before in the east.

The line does not follow 180° exactly because it goes around some island nations so one nation is not split into different days.

⭐ Remember: Cross the Date Line → the day changes.
Lesson 1 • Maps

Why Do We Need Map Projections?

Textbook page 8 • Figure 7

📖 Easy Explanation

Earth is a sphere, but a map is flat.

A projection transfers features from a globe to a flat map.

Globe→Projection→Flat Map

The textbook states that the process always results in some distortion.

👀 Look at the textbook visual

  • The picture shows a cylinder and a cone placed around a globe.
  • Both methods transfer globe features onto a flat surface.
⭐ Remember: Globe → flat map = some distortion.
Lesson 1 • Maps

Cylindrical Projection

Textbook page 8

📖 Easy Explanation

A cylindrical projection is made as if a sheet of paper is wrapped around the globe like a cylinder.

  • Shapes near the equator are represented well.
  • Shapes near the poles are enlarged.

The textbook example says Greenland appears larger than South America, although Greenland is about one-eighth the size of South America.

👀 Look at the textbook visual

  • Focus on the cylinder around the globe.
  • Notice how the flat map is produced from the wrapped surface.
⭐ Remember: Cylindrical: good near equator • enlarged near poles.
Lesson 1 • Maps

Conical Projection

Textbook page 8

📖 Easy Explanation

A conical projection is made by wrapping a cone around the globe.

  • There is little distortion near the line of latitude where the cone touches the globe.
  • It is distorted elsewhere.

The textbook also reminds us that all types of projections distort shapes observed on a sphere.

👀 Look at the textbook visual

  • Focus on the cone touching the globe.
  • The least distortion is near the line where the cone touches.
⭐ Remember: Conical: least distortion near the contact line.

Skill Practice: Map Your Classroom

Textbook page 10

📖 Easy Explanation

The Skill Practice shows how map scale can be used for a real room.

  • Measure the classroom carefully.
  • Choose a scale.
  • Draw the room on graph paper.
  • Include and label features such as doors and windows.

The textbook example explains that if the scale is 1 cm to 1 m, then 5 cm on the map represents 5 m.

👀 Look at the textbook visual

  • The classroom sketch includes measurements and a scale.
  • The drawing keeps the room smaller but proportional.
⭐ Remember: A scaled map keeps distances proportional to the real place.
